title: Justice, again and again
hookLine: justice is commanded again and again, even against yourself (4:135; 5:8)

cards: Being fair is easy when nothing's at stake. It gets hard in three places. When the truth hurts you.
When it hurts someone you love. And when it helps someone you can't stand. It's easy to carve out those three exceptions without ever saying so out loud.
Two verses of the Qur'an close them, one by one, and in that order. The second verse even names the third exception directly: the people you hate.

teach.b: Surah an-Nisa, verse one hundred thirty-five. Believers, be steadfast in justice, witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves, or your parents, or your relatives, whether the person is rich or poor. Look at the order.
Yourself first. Then the people closest to you. Then rich and poor, so you can't favor the powerful or pity your way past the truth either.
Now al-Ma'idah, verse eight, in Pickthall's translation: "Let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly. Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty."
Even the people you hate get a fair hearing. The Qur'an uses two words for this. 'Adl is evenness, setting things level.

Qist carries the picture of a fair share, a fair measure, and the book ties it to the balance and the scales: surah fifty-seven says the messengers were sent with the book and the balance so that people would uphold qist.
Commentators tell a story behind a passage in an-Nisa, around verse one hundred five. A man from a Muslim family stole, and his clan tried to pin it on a Jewish man.
Verses came down clearing the innocent man and warning against pleading for the guilty.
That's the occasion as the commentators report it; the verses themselves speak of not pleading for the treacherous, and of the sin of throwing blame on the innocent. Either way, the pattern holds.
In the Qur'an, justice isn't a feeling about who deserves to win.
It's a scale you hold level, even when your own hand is on one side of it.

how: Muslim jurists treat justice ('adl) as a central aim of Islamic law, and 4:135 and 5:8 are often quoted on fairness in testimony, judging and everyday dealing, including with opponents.

o: loyalty to your own family and side
fairness held level, even against yourself
kindness that forgives and lets things go

p: a fair share, tied to the scales

s: the Qur'an allows favoring family in testimony
4:135 names parents and relatives among those you must be just against.
the Qur'an commands justice even toward a hated people
5:8: let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly.
qist is tied to the picture of scales and balance
the messengers were sent with the book and the balance so people would uphold qist (57:25).

games.q: you're a witness. the truth will cost your own brother. what does 4:135 say?
o: testify truthfully, even against your relatives.
games.why: be steadfast in justice, witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves, your parents or your relatives.

practice: Think of one disagreement in your life right now, and put yourself on the scale first: where was I wrong, even a little?
Then find the strongest true thing on the other person's side, and set it beside yours without arguing it away. If you pray, you can ask to be steadfast in justice.

wordCard.voice: Justice. 'Adl and qist: commanded again and again, against yourself and your family, for rich and poor, and even toward people you dislike. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: justice as a fair share and fair measure.

carryVoice: Your line: stand for justice. Level scales, for friend and stranger alike. See you tomorrow.
